TI Determinants of collaborative learning in online distance education: the
   role of self-efficacy as a mediator
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MOBILE LEARNING AND ORGANISATION
LA English
DT Article
DE collaborative learning; learners' self-efficacy; interaction with
   tutors; interaction with peers; social media usage; social presence
ID SOCIAL PRESENCE; SEM; SUCCESS
AB The study underscores the significance of collaborative learning within flexible online learning environments in higher education institutions (HEIs). It examined the effects of collaborative learning through peer and tutor interactions, social presence, social media use, and self-efficacy as a mediating variable. Data were collected via a structured survey, with 507 questionnaires distributed and 388 analysed. The PLS-SEM method was employed to measure the connections among variables and test the hypotheses. In doing so, HEIs can enhance learning and prepare students for collaborative roles. TI Virtual reality-enhanced learning for ESL/EFL presentation skills:
   effects on holistic learning outcomes
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MOBILE LEARNING AND ORGANISATION
LA English
DT Article
DE ESL/EFL; mobile-assisted language learning; MALL; learning outcomes;
   presentation skills; public speaking; virtual reality; VR
AB This study investigates the potential of a virtual reality (VR) online learning platform, specifically Chill Talk, to enhance presentation skills. Grounded in constructivism, Chill Talk integrated comprehensive learning materials, videos, a forum, and immersive VR presentation practice. It enabled learners to engage in immersive environments and deliver presentations using their own slides, smartphones, and affordable VR devices. Employing a holistic assessment approach, the study examined students' learning outcomes across academic achievement, cognitive development, and affective growth. The participants, ESL/EFL university students in Hong Kong, used Chill Talk for self-directed English presentation learning and practice over two months. Pre- and post-study surveys were conducted to collect both quantitative and qualitative data. The results revealed that Chill Talk significantly enhanced all perceived learning outcomes. Academically, participants demonstrated improved language proficiency, presentation skills, and reduced public-speaking anxiety. Moreover, it facilitated cognitive and affective development, including metacognitive ability, critical thinking, motivation, engagement, and confidence.

TI Eat, play, discover: a cross-cultural serious game for children's
   self-exploration and nutritional awareness
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF MOBILE LEARNING AND ORGANISATION
LA English
DT Article
DE serious game; gamified learning; nutrition education; cross-cultural
   learning; self-exploration; game design; children;
   mechanics-dynamics-aesthetics; MDA
ID MOBILE GAME
AB This study introduces a cross-cultural serious game called 'All You Can Eat', which combines food culture content with engaging gameplay to educate children aged 7 to 12 learn about healthy eating and balanced meals. The game uses the mechanics-dynamics-aesthetics (MDA) approach, with three main actions: eat, digest, and balance. With help from the 'My Plate' model, players collect tokens for six food groups to learn about the right food portions and how to avoid overeating or undereating. A total of 94 students aged 9 to 12 participated in the study. The research methodology included a pre-test, gameplay session, and post-test to assess learning outcomes. The results showed significant improvements in children's nutritional knowledge, food choices, and daily use of what they learned. Additionally, the game's global food cards also made children more interested in different food cultures, such as Asian, Middle Eastern, and Western dishes. This study demonstrates that game-based learning can be an effective way to teach nutrition and help children build healthy eating habits.

TI Scaffolding early-stage simultaneous interpreting learning using
   computerized dynamic assessment
SO LANGUAGE LEARNING & TECHNOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE adaptive scaffolding; computerized dynamic assessment; simultaneous
   interpreting; syntactic complexity; fluency
ID COGNITIVE LOAD; PERFORMANCE; COMPLEXITY; FLUENCY; ANXIETY
AB Computerized Dynamic Assessment (CDA) integrates assessment and instruction by algorithmically delivering immediate, adaptive scaffolding to uncover and cultivate learners' developmental potential. Although CDA has shown promise for receptive language skills (e.g., reading and listening), its effectiveness in simultaneous interpreting (SI) remains underexplored. As a high-stakes bilingual task, SI requires the concurrent processing of source-language input and target-language output, rendering it both cognitively taxing and anxiety-inducing. To address this gap, the present study employed a pretest-intervention-posttest design with 35 novice SI learners from two intact classes, with one class serving as the CDA group (n = 18) and the other as the non-CDA group (n = 17). The CDA group received adaptive, graduated scaffolding targeting five types of complex syntactic structures, whereas the non-CDA group received static, non-graduated support. Interpreting performance was assessed using seven complexity, accuracy, and fluency (CAF) indices, and interpreting-specific anxiety was measured with a Likert-scale questionnaire. Results indicated that the CDA group achieved significantly greater gains in syntactic complexity and fluency and reported lower interpreting anxiety; by contrast, improvements in accuracy were comparable between groups. Overall, these findings provide empirical evidence that the benefits of CDA extend beyond receptive skills to facilitate integrative, real-time oral production under combined cognitive and affective pressure.

TI The development of EFL learners' self-efficacy in technology use
   environments
SO LANGUAGE LEARNING & TECHNOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE technology use; self-efficacy; four sources; metacognitive dimensions of
   mastery experiences; cognitive dimensions of mastery experiences
ID BELIEFS
AB Self-efficacy plays a critical role in language learning motivation, performance, and achievement. However, limited research has examined how different dimensions of English self-efficacy evolve over time and the mechanisms underlying such development in technology use environments. To address these gaps, the present study adopted a mixed-methods design. A total of 102 university students completed questionnaires at three time points over a 15-week period, and 10 participants subsequently took part in semi-structured follow-up interviews. Quantitative findings revealed a significant increase in overall English self-efficacy, as well as in three specific dimensions: speaking, listening, and writing self-efficacy. Qualitative findings further demonstrated how the four sources of self-efficacy, shaped by technological affordances, were associated with students' efficacy beliefs and helped explain why reading self-efficacy did not show a statistically significant increase within the same learning ecology. The study concluded by discussing pedagogical implications for strengthening reading self-efficacy and optimizing the use of technology in language learning, as well as limitations of the study and directions for future research.

TI Teacher Education Reforms and Institutional Change: Insights from the
   Faure Report and the Spanish Case
SO REVISTA COMPLUTENSE DE EDUCACION
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE teacher education; educational reform; educational policy; institutional
   change; UNESCO
AB The reform of teacher education has been a central concern in international educational policy since the second half of the twentieth century. The UNESCO Faure Report (1972) identified key trends in this field, particularly the pedagogical orientation of teacher training and the need for institutional integration. This study examines how these trends influenced the Spanish educational reform introduced by the General Education Law (1970) and its subsequent development. A historical analysis based on primary and secondary sources, including UNESCO documents, legislative records, and archival materials, is conducted. The findings show that while the Spanish reform aligned with the international trends identified in the Faure Report, it did so in a limited and uneven way. In particular, the persistence of institutional dualism in teacher education and the separation between pedagogical research and practice have remained significant challenges over time. The study provides historically grounded insights into current debates on teacher education reform, highlighting the long-term implications of institutional design and the difficulties of achieving coherent and integrated training models.

TI Game-based learning strategies: a typological proposition through a
   hermeneutic approach
SO REVISTA IBERO-AMERICANA DE ESTUDOS EM EDUCACAO
LA English
DT Article
DE Game-Based Learning (GBL); commercial games in education; pedagogical
   strategy; typological classification
AB Although the use of digital and analog games in education is increasing, the term Game-Based Learning (GBL) remains imprecise in the literature and is frequently confused with gamification and serious games. This ambiguity hinders the adoption of structured pedagogical approaches based on commercial entertainment games. The present study distinguishes GBL from other game-related educational strategies and proposes a typology grounded in the pedagogical intentionality attributed to commercial entertainment games within formal or semi-formal educational contexts. Adopting a hermeneutic approach, the study identifies recurring forms of pedagogical appropriation and organizes them into three proposed strategies: (1) Games to Foster Interest, (2) Games as Platforms for Skill and Competency Development, and (3) Modified Games. To illustrate the applicability of the proposed typology, the study presents a multivocal mapping of educational uses of commercial entertainment games across different contexts. The analysis indicates that these approaches are already present in educational practice, although they are rarely systematized or clearly differentiated in the literature. The proposed typology offers a conceptual and practical reference to support both teaching practice and future research.

TI IKEA Effect in the Evaluation of Academic Assignments
SO VOPROSY OBRAZOVANIYA-EDUCATIONAL STUDIES MOSCOW
LA English
DT Article
DE academic assignments; final projects; behavioral economics; IKEA effect
ID PSYCHOLOGICAL OWNERSHIP; DECISION
AB The IKEA effect refers to a cognitive bias whereby people tend to overvalue products or outcomes they have contributed effort to. This study examines how this bias manifests itself in academic settings, specifically in the evaluation of student assignments. The research consists of three studies: the first one analyzed 115 final projects and found that academic advisors consistently graded their own students' work higher than did external evaluators - on average, by about 5%. The second and third studies showed that students also tended to rate their own assignments more generously than their peers or instructors did. These findings point to a systematic bias in academic assessment that has implications not only for fairness but also for the long-term integrity of academic evaluation systems. By highlighting the role of subjective involvement in shaping evaluation outcomes, the study contributes to broader discussions about sustainability in education - particularly in the context of maintaining fair, transparent, and trust-based assessment practices.

TI Applying Peer Instruction to Teaching Physics in Grade 7: Impact on
   Student Achievement and Misconceptions
SO VOPROSY OBRAZOVANIYA-EDUCATIONAL STUDIES MOSCOW
LA English
DT Article
DE alternative conceptions; peer teaching method; physics performance;
   understanding
ID CONCEPTUAL CHANGE; STATIC EQUILIBRIUM; ENERGY; MOMENTUM; STABILITY;
   FRAMEWORK; EDUCATION
AB Considering the challenges students face in learning physics, exploring the use of peer instruction in primary school could provide teachers with a valuable new teaching strategy. This research encompassed teaching the topics Balance and Energy, with the aim of examining the impact of peer instruction on student achievement and its role in reducing misconceptions. The respondents were 132 Grade 7 students (13 years old) from two primary schools in Subotica, Republic of Serbia. A pedagogical experiment was conducted with an experimental and control group, using a pretest-posttest design. Statistical analysis included the Mann-Whitney U test, independent samples t-test, paired samples t-test, and calculation of n-gain and the percentage of students understanding the concepts. The results showed that the application of peer instruction leads to better student achievement (the t-test results showed a significant difference between the experimental and control groups at the end of the pedagogical experiment, t = -3.86, p < 0.001), however does not spontaneously lead to a reduction in misconceptions (Man-Whitney U test showed no significant difference in misconceptions between groups after the pedagogical experiment, U = 721.50, p = 0.432). Additionally, this teaching method is equally effective in fostering deeper learning and engagement for both genders.

TI A Multidisciplinary ICU Clerkship Curriculum Incorporating Simulation
   and Competency-Based Education: Design, Implementation, and Early
   Outcomes
SO ADVANCES IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE critical care education; undergraduate medical education; clerkship
   curriculum; simulation-based learning; competency-based assessment
AB Introduction: Critical care competencies are increasingly relevant across specialties, yet structured exposure in undergraduate medical education (UME) remains variable. We describe the design, implementation, and early outcomes of a four-week, modular ICU clerkship.<br /> Methods: We implemented a multidisciplinary ICU clerkship integrating clinical immersion, protected weekly didactics, asynchronous learning, high-fidelity simulation, health equity rounds, and palliative care debriefing. Objectives were aligned with Delphi-derived undergraduate critical care competencies and AAMC Entrustable Professional Activities. We compared student clerkship evaluation ratings (learner perceptions on a 5-point Likert scale) before and after a comprehensive curriculum redesign (July 2022-June 2024 vs July 2024-June 2025) using Welch two-sample t-tests.<br /> Results: Approximately 95 students per year completed the clerkship. Following redesign, the largest improvements were observed in structural and organizational domains: orientation (+0.94), syllabus (+0.95), didactics (+0.85), and organization (+0.76) (all p < 0.001). Clinical skills (+0.36, p=0.01) and knowledge (+0.31, p=0.01) increased modestly and remained consistently high. Simulation ratings remained high (4.44 to 4.65, p=0.04). Overall clerkship rating improved from 4.00 to 4.51 (p=0.002).<br /> Discussion: A modular ICU clerkship is feasible and adaptable across settings. Improvements were most pronounced in structural domains, while core clinical learning domains remained stable, suggesting that targeted curricular redesign can enhance learner experience while maintaining high perceived educational value.

TI Development of a Simulation-Based Educational Intervention to Improve
   Nursing Competencies for Stroke Care in Southwestern Uganda
SO ADVANCES IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE stroke care; simulation educational interventions; nursing; Uganda
ID KNOWLEDGE
AB Introduction: Stroke is one of the leading causes of disability worldwide, and its prevalence is increasing in low- and middle-income countries (LMIC) like Uganda, presenting nursing care challenges. Simulation-based learning has been used successfully to train nurses in general care in LMIC but has not been applied to training for stroke care. In this study, we aimed to develop a simulationbased stroke care education intervention for nurses involved in care for patients with stroke at a large hospital in southwestern Uganda. Methods: Between February 2024 and March 2025, we used the iterative design to develop an educational intervention for stroke care. We engaged stroke care content experts through in-depth qualitative interviews (n=14), generated content, and developed the first version of the intervention. Transcripts were derived, reviewed and coded to generate themes and categories using inductive content analytic approach. We then tested, analyzed and refined the intervention through three repetitive exposures of the intervention to final year Bachelor of Nursing students (n=20), with improvements after every exposure. That were grouped in teams of 5 students. Results: Qualitative data from content experts revealed three thematic areas of patient care including admission of a stroke patient, care for a stroke patient during their hospital stay and discharge of a stroke patient as key content for consideration during intervention development. This content was integrated into the "Uganda Simulation-Based Nursing Stroke Care intervention". Post-exposure qualitative interviews with final year Bachelor of Nursing students revealed great satisfaction with the intervention, improved preparedness and ease to assess stroke patients. There were also high teamwork scores and improved clinical skills. To maintain efficiency with stroke care competencies, they preferred at least three exposures to the intervention per year. Conclusion: With diverse stakeholders, we used an iterative approach to develop a context specific, simulation-based stroke educational intervention. Future work will examine the feasibility, acceptability, and effectiveness of this intervention among nurses working with stroke patients and its effect on the patient outcomes.

TI Predictors of Considering a Vascular Surgery Career Among Medical
   Students at Jazan University, Saudi Arabia: A Cross-Sectional Study
SO ADVANCES IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE vascular surgery; medical students; career choice; specialty preference;
   Saudi Arabia
ID PERCEPTIONS; RESIDENTS; SPECIALTY; CHOICE
AB Background: Vascular surgery faces a sustained workforce shortage worldwide, with persistent gender disparities in the international pipeline. This study characterized medical students' knowledge and perceptions of vascular surgery at Jazan University and identified factors independently associated with having considered a vascular surgery career. Methods: A cross-sectional study used a 34-item questionnaire among fourth- to sixth-year medical students. Bivariate analyses used Mann-Whitney U and Kruskal-Wallis tests, and the primary outcome was modeled with multivariable binary logistic regression on pre-specified predictors. Results: Of 213 respondents (54.9% male; mean age 22.9 +/- 1.4 years), 43 (20.2%) had considered a vascular surgery career. In the adjusted model, male gender was the strongest independent predictor of the outcome (aOR 4.55; 95% CI 1.84-11.24; p = 0.001), and greater importance attached to training length was associated with lower odds (aOR 0.63; 95% CI 0.42-0.96; p = 0.030). Female students scored lower than male students on the Perceptions of Vascular Surgeons composite (3.06 +/- 0.54 vs. 3.25 +/- 0.42; p < 0.001). Lifestyle as an attending was the highest-rated specialty-selection factor (4.27 +/- 1.07), yet only 11.3% agreed that vascular surgeons have a good work-life balance and only 21.6% agreed the career offers adequate family time. Self-rated knowledge was low (2.86 +/- 0.88) but rose with educational stage (p < 0.001). Conclusion: Male gender was the strongest independent predictor of having considered a vascular surgery career, with over four-and -a-half times the odds of female students. Self-rated knowledge was low despite structured teaching, and perceptions of work-life balance were negative, mirroring international findings. Strengthening the depth and clinical immersion of existing vascular surgery teaching, establishing a vascular surgery interest group, and providing female-oriented mentorship are evidence-based next steps for the Saudi vascular surgery community.

TI Where Does Data Science Live in High School Curricular Standards?
SO AERA OPEN
LA English
DT Article
DE high schools; curriculum; standard setting; qualitative research; data
   science education; NGSS; CSTA; CCSS; C3 Framework for Social Studies
AB Integrating data science into K-12 education requires accommodating its interdisciplinary nature in the traditionally subject-based curriculum structure. This makes it essential to examine how existing educational standards adequately support or fall short of supporting the learning of data science. This study investigates how data science concepts align with five nationwide educational standards for grades 9-12 in the United States: the Computer Science Teachers Association standards, the Next Generation Science Standards, Common Core State Standards for Mathematics and for English Language Arts and Literacy, and the College, Career, and Civic Life Framework for Social Studies. We conduct qualitative content analysis to identify the manifest and latent connections between the five standards and core data science topics. The findings reveal opportunities and challenges for the interdisciplinary integration of data science content both within and across subjects, providing a foundation for developing future integration roadmaps.

TI Go Buya as a Tool for Culturally Sustaining Pedagogy in Indigenous and
   Borderland Education
SO BROCK EDUCATION-A JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE Indigenous lifelong learning; culturally sustaining teaching; civic
   literacy; game-based learning; Dayak education; borderland teaching
AB Indigenous lifelong learning is based on passing down knowledge between generations, maintaining cultural traditions, and education connected to specific places. In the borderland area of Entikong, Indonesia, Indigenous Dayak communities face systemic obstacles to getting an education that respects their culture. They often come across curricula that overlook their heritage. This study presents Go Buya, a game-based learning tool created with the help of local elders, educators, and cultural practitioners to connect traditional knowledge with formal education. Grounded in a culturally sustaining teaching approach, Go Buya weaves Dayak stories, symbols, and civic issues into the gameplay. This approach promotes student engagement, affirms identity, and encourages critical thinking about civic duties. Using a Design and Development Research methodology, the project took place in three stages: community consultation, game design, and classroom testing in three borderland schools. The results showed an increase in student curiosity, intergenerational conversations, and collaborative learning, which are essential parts of Indigenous lifelong learning. Students examined their civic duties through culturally relevant scenarios, building relational accountability and ethical thinking. This study highlights the promise of cultural tools to revive Indigenous education in underserved areas. Go Buya serves as a model for how Indigenous knowledge can shape new teaching methods, support cultural survival, and encourage lifelong learning in Indigenous and international communities.

TI Online Higher Education for Indigenous Students: Between Digital
   Colonization and Opportunity
SO BROCK EDUCATION-A JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE Indigenous students; higher education; online learning; digital divide;
   decolonizing education; Indigenous sovereignty
ID EXPERIENCES; 1ST
AB Online higher education is often framed as a flexible and equitable pathway to postsecondary education. For Indigenous students, however, digital learning environments exist at the intersection of opportunity and ongoing colonial harm. This literature review critically examines research published since 2014 on Indigenous students' experiences in online higher education. Guided by Indigenous sovereignty, relational accountability, and digital divide theory, the review synthesizes findings related to infrastructure and access, cultural and pedagogical alignment, psychological and social dimensions of learning, and Indigenous-centred approaches to online course design. The literature suggests that dominant online learning models frequently reproduce Eurocentric assumptions that marginalize Indigenous epistemologies, contributing to diminished belonging, lower persistence, and widened achievement gaps. At the same time, studies highlight the potential of online education to foster access, cultural resurgence, and self-determination when learning environments are developed in partnership with Indigenous communities and grounded in relational pedagogies. The review concludes that online learning is not inherently colonizing; rather, its effects are shaped by the epistemological frameworks that guide its design and implementation. Implications include the need for Indigenous-led digital education, greater attention to Indigenous data sovereignty and disaggregation, and sovereignty-affirming approaches to emerging technologies.

TI Indigenous Knowledge and Lifelong Learning: Towards a Decolonial
   Framework for Epistemic Justice in South Africa
SO BROCK EDUCATION-A JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE Indigenous knowledge systems; lifelong learning; decolonization;
   epistemic justice; Ubuntu pedagogy; adult education; South Africa
AB Indigenous knowledge systems (IKS) remain marginalized in mainstream education despite their potential to enrich lifelong learning pathways and strengthen cultural identity. This conceptual paper argues for a decolonial framework that repositions IKS as central to educational design across the lifespan, from early childhood through adult and community learning. Drawing on decolonial theory, Ubuntu pedagogy, and critical Indigenous scholarship, the paper explores how Indigenous epistemologies can foster self-directed learning, intergenerational knowledge transfer, and resilience in marginalized communities. A systematic reading of scholarship on IKS integration highlights persistent barriers: policy centralization, Western epistemic dominance, and insufficient teacher preparation. To address these challenges, the paper proposes a three-dimensional framework for decolonial lifelong learning: (a) Epistemic Inclusion, embedding IKS as valid and legitimate knowledge; (b) Pedagogical Plurality, incorporating land-based, oral, and spiritual ways of knowing alongside formal schooling; and (c) Community Co-creation, positioning elders and local practitioners as co-educators. This framework not only contributes to epistemic justice in South Africa but also resonates with global debates on Indigenous rights and sustainable education. The paper concludes that reimagining lifelong learning through Indigenous knowledge is essential for addressing inequities and for cultivating future-oriented, culturally sustaining education systems.

TI "Someone Invested in Me": Learning Through High School Co-operative
   Education
SO BROCK EDUCATION-A JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE work-based education; co-operative education; co-workers; social
   belonging; persistence in high school
ID TO-WORK TRANSITION; AT-RISK YOUTH; EPISTEMOLOGICAL APPROPRIATION;
   WORKPLACE; STUDENTS; PARTICIPATION; MODEL
AB Co-operative (co-op) education is a type of work-based education in which senior high school students are placed in supervised workplace settings and gain credits towards a graduation diploma. This study presents the perceptions of three participants in co-op education workplaces, how they learned, and the influence of their co-workers. The theoretical lenses providing the structure and focus of this research were Billet's (2014) theory of mimesis, Munby et al.'s (2003) theory of metacognitive routines, and Snyder's (2000) hope theory. Three former high school students (one with an IEP and two at risk of dropping out) who had been in automotive co-op education placements participated in semi-structured interviews. The results showed that the participants valued the skills that were taught in the workplace, and learning involved co-workers who provided individual instruction consisting of observing, imitating, and receiving feedback. The co-workers created a supportive social environment, and their interaction with the students resulted in feelings of social belonging, success, as well as the motivation and hope to graduate high school and develop career goals.

TI Participation or Performance? Critical Reflections on "Take Our Kids to
   Work Day" and Reconceptualization Through a Child Rights Lens
SO BROCK EDUCATION-A JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE child protection; child rights; education
AB Canada's national initiative, "Take Our Kids to Work Day" (TKWD), celebrated its 30th anniversary in 2024. The annual event allows Grade 9 students across the country an opportunity to spend the day at work with important adults, and to learn workplace skills in lieu of attending school. Despite its long tenure, there is an apparent gap in the current body of academic scholarship focused on young people's perceptions of TKWD. For many young people, this initiative offers a first glimpse into the workplace skills and opportunities available to them. This conceptual paper is co-authored by a mother and daughter and utilizes reflexivity as a method to include the critical reflections and voice of a youth co-author who participated in TKWD in two distinct workplace contexts: child welfare and academia. As mother-daughter participants, the co-authors' experience with TKWD was generally positive; however, we suggest the initiative could be improved. In (re)conceptualizing TKWD through a child rights lens, we argue young people must be active participants, and afforded opportunities to provide feedback in a meaningful way.

TI Preservice Early-Grade Teachers' Perception of Play-Based Learning (PBL)
   in Mathematics Education
SO BROCK EDUCATION-A JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE preservice; teacher; early-grade; play-based-learning; mathematics
   education
ID PEDAGOGY; CHILD
AB The study examines preservice early-grade teachers' perceptions of play-based learning (PBL) in teaching mathematics, focusing on its effectiveness and alignment with curriculum demands. Using a cross-sectional survey, data were collected from 150 preservice teachers in Ghana's Upper West Region through a structured questionnaire. The data collected were analyzed using descriptive (mean and median) and inferential statistics (Kruskal-Wallis and Mann-Whitney U tests) via SPSS. The study's findings revealed that preservice teachers view PBL as beneficial for engagement and conceptual understanding, but they face challenges in balancing it with structured curricula. Educational level influences perceptions, while sex does not. The study highlights the need for structured PBL integration in teacher education programs.

TI Relational Practices and School Climate: An Ethnographic Study in TDSB
   High Schools
SO BROCK EDUCATION-A JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE school climate; relational trust; Occasional Teachers; Indigenous
   pedagogies; decolonizing education
AB This ethnographic study explores how relational practices such as inclusive communication, peer support, interdepartmental cooperation, and leadership visibility influence school climate and culture across eight high schools within the Toronto District School Board (TDSB), Ontario, Canada. Drawing from the unique dual perspective of the researcher, an Assistant Professor and certified occasional teacher, the study provides situated observations collected over a 2-month period in the 2024-2025 school year. The findings are based on anecdotal field notes gathered during regular teaching assignments in varied school contexts, including inner-city and affluent schools with diverse student populations. Thematic analysis revealed three central themes: inclusive communication and trust-building; peer support and informal collaboration; and shared leadership through interdepartmental cooperation. Visibility and relational leadership from school administration were positively correlated with school-wide engagement and student well-being, while their absence often aligned with lower morale and cohesion. The study also considers Indigenous pedagogies as frameworks for fostering relationality and inclusivity. Implications for teacher education, leadership development, and culturally responsive school practices are discussed, with recommendations for future research to explore these dynamics longitudinally and across broader school systems.

TI Educating Cities: An Analysis of 47 Experiences Highlighted by the IAEC
   in Light of the Public Policy Cycle and the Principles of the Charter of
   Educating Cities
SO BROCK EDUCATION-A JOURNAL OF EDUCATIONAL RESEARCH AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE educating cities; public policy; urban education
AB The concept of educating cities acknowledges that education transcends school boundaries, permeating the urban space and involving multiple social actors. The International Association of Educating Cities (IAEC) promotes and documents transformative initiatives worldwide. This article aims to analyze 47 experiences highlighted by the IAEC, focusing on implemented actions, mobilized principles, challenges encountered, and results achieved, based on the public policy cycle framework. This is a qualitative-quantitative, exploratory, and descriptive study based on content analysis of documents published by the IAEC. The cases were analyzed according to the Educating Cities Charter principles and the five stages of the public policy cycle. Findings reveal strong adherence to principles such as lifelong learning, cultural access, and democratic citizenship. Civil society organizations and educational institutions played a key role in implementation. However, themes like sustainability, social responsibility, and citizen participation remain underrepresented. Challenges include resource constraints, institutional conflicts, and lack of sustainability planning. The cases analyzed demonstrate significant progress and innovative practices but also highlight the need for greater balance in principle application and improved formulation and evaluation stages. This study contributes to strengthening the network of educating cities and supports the development of more equitable and integrated urban education policies

TI Assessment and rubrics in the LLSS translation classroom
SO INTERCAMBIOS-DILEMAS Y TRANSICIONES DE LA EDUCACION SUPERIOR
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE didactics of translation; sign languages; formative assessment; rubric
AB The training of translators and interpreters of sign languages (LLSS) in the university environment demands demands in terms of teacher training and aspects related to the didactic field of study of translation. Evaluations in this context represent a challenge for teachers, due to the diversity of versions present in a translation, and it makes the task of assessing student learning based on clear parameters more complex. In this sense, this article focuses on systematizing the use of rubrics as an instrument of continuous evaluation of the performance of students of the LSU-Spanish Interpreting and Translation Technologist program at the Faculty of Humanities and Educational Sciences. This evaluative approach is articulated with the competency approach, whose objective is to develop linguistic, intercultural and translational competencies, essential for the training of translators and interpreters. The application of rubrics as an evaluation tool in translation programs whose linguistic combination involves sign languages will be addressed, recognizing that rubrics are a resource that guides students and allows them to identify areas for improvement. The development of the rubrics was based on the parameters established in the new Udelar grading scale (2018, 2020), under the premise that an evaluation of a conceptual nature is aligned to the qualitative and formative approaches to evaluation.

TI Psychology of, and, in education. Epistemic
   positions in higher education in Argentina on the articulations between
   psychology and education
SO INTERCAMBIOS-DILEMAS Y TRANSICIONES DE LA EDUCACION SUPERIOR
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE psychology; psychoanalysis; education; professional intervention;
   pedagogical discourse
AB This essay aims, in general terms, to trace the epistemic positions regarding the connections between Psychology, Psychoanalysis and Education at the Higher University Level in Argentina. To this end, we will first define what an epistemic position is and how it differs from an epistemological perspective. Second, we will establish the epistemic positions at the Higher University Level in relation to the use of the words "of", "and", or "in", since these reflect the discipline's relationship to the field of intervention. TI The influence of digital literacy training on self-efficacy, digital

DT Article

   VALIDATION; BARRIERS; PROGRAMS; DIVIDE; BIAS
AB Digital literacy training (DLT) is paramount in equipping individuals with knowledge and skills necessary to navigate the online landscape. While existing literature has extensively explored the roles of self-efficacy (SE) and digital literacy skills (DLS) in influencing digital engagements and, subsequently, internet outcome (IO) achievement, there is a notable gap in understanding how DLT directly affects IO achievement. TI Lost in transition: a mixed-methods study on students' experiences and
   challenges migrating between learning management systems in higher
   education
SO INTERNATIONAL JOURNAL OF LEARNING TECHNOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE learning management system; LMSs; transition; migration; students;
   higher education; mixed-methods
ID SELF-EFFICACY; PERCEPTIONS; SATISFACTION; TECHNOLOGY; CONTINUANCE
AB With the increasing reliance on learning management systems (LMSs) to support online and blended-learning in higher education, the adoption/switch to a new system can disrupt student learning. This mixed-methods study explored 128 students' reflections of an institution-wide transition from blackboard to canvas, and whether individual characteristics (self-efficacy, technology anxiety, personality) predicted positive experiences. Positive LMS transition experiences were predicted by higher online-learning self-efficacy and lower technology anxiety, but not personality. Overall ratings of the transition were moderately negative due to lack of awareness and understanding of why the transition occurred, lack of staff confidence and knowledge about the new system, and lack of consistency across courses and systems. Interestingly, these concerns were consistent among students regardless of their level of online-learning self-efficacy and technology anxiety. This study contributes to the academic discourse on technological transitions for online and blended-learning in higher education and provides guidance for institutions planning system changes.

TI 'It's actually changed my perspective': spaces for genuine dialogic
   surprise within the initial teacher education curriculum
SO LONDON REVIEW OF EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Martin Buber; dialogism; primary education; ITT policy; curriculum
   design
AB In this article, we draw on Martin Buber's idea of dialogical surprise in educational experiences to consider curriculum design in initial teacher education. We argue that the current policy environment in England fosters a monological approach, stifling meaning-making and innovation. Contributing to conversations around initial teacher education curriculum design within a constricted policy environment in England, the research presents findings on initial teacher education curriculum experiences of Year 3 Primary Education undergraduate student teachers who completed one of three module electives (Thinking and Philosophy for Children; Creativity in Education; Early Years Education). These modules form part of the wider initial teacher education curriculum design at the institution in which the research was undertaken, aiming to develop student teachers' critical thinking, reflection and personal philosophies. The study investigates student teachers' reflections on participating in dialogue, which involves recognising their own and other perspectives. When curriculum design enabled spaces for new meanings to emerge, the possibility for an interplay of voices was allowed. Arguing that dialogic spaces are effectively closed down within the Department for Education's main prescribed initial teacher education framework, we add our voices to the urgent call for a less prescriptive framework which recognises the professional expertise of teacher educators in curriculum design.

TI Midday educational time in primary education. A participatory evaluation
   using the Photovoice methodology
SO RIE-REVISTA DE INVESTIGACION EDUCATIVA
LA English
DT Article
DE primary education; school canteen; child well-being; photovoice
AB Midday educational time in primary education is a key moment for children's personal, social, emotional, and educational development. However, its pedagogical value has rarely been evaluated from the students' perspective. This study, commissioned by a third-sector organization and conducted by an interdisciplinary team from the Faculties of Psychology and Education at the University of Barcelona, analyzes what learning children identify in this time and what factors facilitate or hinder it through a participatory evaluation based on the Photovoice methodology. Five schools in Catalonia participated, with 50 fourth- and fifth-grade students who generated photographs and narratives that were analyzed using inductive thematic analysis. The results show that children learn about social interaction and social-emotional skills; participation and engagement; positive time and space management; and nutrition education and sustainability. Key facilitators include variety of activities, suitable spaces, and opportunities for participation. Barriers include conflicts among peers, infrastructure limitations, repetitive menus, and limited child participation in organizational decisions. The study demonstrates the potential of Photovoice to incorporate children's voices into evaluation processes and provides evidence for rethinking midday educational time as a comprehensive pedagogical space focused on personal development, well-being, and child participation.

TI Beyond the White Coat: A Multispecialty Needs Assessment of Residents'
   Teaching Perceptions Competency, and Learning Needs
SO ADVANCES IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE residents as teachers; medical education; clinical teaching; learning
   needs; interprofessional education
ID MEDICAL-EDUCATION; TEACHERS; SKILLS; ROLES
AB Background: Residents contribute substantially to clinical teaching; however, many lack formal preparation for their role as educators. Despite rising expectations within competency frameworks, evidence from multicultural, rapidly evolving training environments remains limited. This study aimed to assess residents' perceptions of their educator role, evaluate self-reported teaching competency and involvement, and identify learning needs to inform the development of a context-sensitive Residents-as-Teachers program. Methods: A cross-sectional needs assessment survey was conducted among all 322 medical and surgical residents in a large academic health system between May and July 2025. A validated, locally adapted questionnaire assessed perceptions, teaching involvement, and learning needs. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics, bivariate analyses, and multivariable linear regression to identify independent predictors of positive perceptions of the educator role. Results: A total of 291 residents participated (response rate 90.4%), representing 18 specialties across medical and surgical disciplines. Residents reported spending a mean of 35.8% of their training time engaged in teaching activities. Overall perceptions of the educator role were positive (mean total score 49.99/60), while self-reported teaching competency was moderate. A consistent interprofessional teaching gap was identified, with nurses ranked least frequently taught by over 80% of residents and receiving the lowest competency rating. Residents expressed strong interest in structured teaching-skills training, preferring interactive instructor-led formats over online self-paced learning. In multivariable regression, interest in a future educator role (p <0.001) and competency in teaching medical students (p =0.038) were the strongest independent predictors of positive educator perceptions. Conclusion: These preliminary findings indicate that residents play a substantial yet underprepared role in clinical teaching. Results suggest that structured, contextually responsive Residents-as-Teachers programs prioritizing motivation, teaching competency, and interprofessional education may help address identified gaps and support the development of future clinician-educators. Longitudinal and implementation-focused research is needed to evaluate whether such programs improve observed teaching performance and learner outcomes in diverse postgraduate training environments.

TI Hotspot Evolution and Future Prospects of Large Language Models in
   Medical Education: A Bibliometric Analysis
SO ADVANCES IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE large language models; artificial intelligence; medical education;
   bibliometric analysis; research trends
ID SCIENCE; WEB
AB Background: Advances in AI and NLP have popularized large language models (LLMs) in medical education. Post-2022 research has proliferated yet remains fragmented; no comprehensive bibliometric mapping systematically outlines this field's global layout, collaboration networks and thematic evolution. Objective: To clarify publication trends, core contributors, collaboration patterns, research hotspots and evolutionary frontiers of LLMs in medical education via bibliometric analysis, and deliver targeted insights for educational practice. Methods: This is a systematic bibliometric study. We collected 2016-March 2026 peer-reviewed English papers from WoSCC and Scopus. Metadata were standardized and analyzed with the Bibliometrix R package and VOSviewer to generate publication statistics, collaboration networks, citation metrics and keyword cluster maps. Results: In total, 1991 papers were included, with an annual growth rate of 59.04%. The US (28.5%) and China (15.9%) led global outputs; Harvard, the University of Toronto and top Chinese scholars dominated contributions, and JMIR Medical Education served as the core journal. Five thematic clusters were identified: education ethics, LLM performance, patient education, clinical reasoning and intelligent assessment. Research priorities shifted from basic neural network exploration to privacy and standardized large-scale LLM deployment after 2024. Conclusion: LLM medical education research grows rapidly but suffers insufficient empirical evidence, unbalanced themes and delayed governance frameworks. Based on our bibliometric findings, we propose practical optimization schemes: strengthen interdisciplinary research, build matched risk supervision, define LLMs as teaching assistants, and prioritize cohort trials, specialized medical LLMs and unified ethical standards. Academic Contributions: This study provides the latest full-spectrum quantitative mapping of the field, fills gaps in systematic literature review, and offers actionable references for medical educators, curriculum developers and policymakers to realize safe, highquality LLM integration into medical education.

TI Knowledge Acquisition, Self-Assessed Competence, and Simulator-Based
   Performance in a Structured Laparoscopic VR Curriculum for Obstetrics
   and Gynecology Residents: A Single-Center Observational Study
SO ADVANCES IN MEDICAL EDUCATION AND PRACTICE
LA English
DT Article
DE laparoscopy/education; gynecology/education; simulation/training;
   clinical competence
ID VIRTUAL-REALITY SIMULATION; SURGERY
AB Introduction: Simulation enables safe, structured practice of laparoscopic skills outside the operating room, yet objective, threshold-referenced performance data from mandatory postgraduate curricula in Central and Eastern Europe remain scarce. We report the educational outcomes of a structured, multi-level virtual-reality (VR) laparoscopy curriculum delivered at a single national simulation center.<br /> Methods: We conducted a single-center prospective observational study of 29 obstetrics and gynecology residents who completed a four-module laparoscopic course (Basic 1- 2, Advanced 1- 2) at the Centre for Endoscopy Simulation, Centre of Postgraduate Medical Education (CMKP), Warsaw. Outcomes comprised pre- and post-course single-choice knowledge tests, self-assessed competence, satisfaction, and simulator-based performance evaluated against a priori, criterion-referenced passing thresholds. Technical metrics were simulator-generated (Simbionix LAP Mentor); no human global rating scales were used. Demographic and training-related variables (gender, residency year, training-center referral level, prior endoscopic experience) were analyzed with non-parametric statistics.<br /> Results: Knowledge scores improved from 20.9 (SD = 2.70) to 29.2 (SD = 1.01) (Wilcoxon, p < 0.05). Self-assessed competence increased significantly across all domains (p < 0.05). Satisfaction was uniformly high (mean 4.7/5, SD = 0.45) but did not correlate with objective performance (all p > 0.05). Outcomes did not differ by gender or training-center referral level; residency year was associated with performance only in colpotomy (rho = - 0.37, p =0.047), and prior experience predicted performance mainly in basic camera manipulation (e.g. 30 degrees navigation distance, rho = - 0.50, p =0.005), consistent with a learning-curve effect.<br /> Conclusion: A structured, multi-modular VR laparoscopy course significantly improved theoretical knowledge and self-assessed competence among OB-GYN residents. Within this single-center cohort, measured outcomes did not differ by gender or training-center referral level. High satisfaction diverged from objective performance, underscoring the need for balanced, criterion-referenced evaluation. A priori passing thresholds enabled transparent, proficiency-oriented assessment.

TI Digital Exhaustion: Exploring Technofatigue and Technostress in Future
   English Teachers
SO ANDEAN JOURNAL OF EDUCATION
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE technofatigue; technostress; cognitive overload; higher education;
   English teacher training
AB This study analyzes the impact of digital technology on the mental and physical health of future university English teachers, focusing on technofatigue and technostress. It highlights the ubiquity of technology and how its excessive use can negatively affect health. The main objective is to examine the relationship between the use of digital technologies and their effects on mental and physical wellbeing within the university educational context. Based on Cognitive Load Theory, the study explains exhaustion resulting from information overload, defining technostress as the difficulty of adapting to technological demands, and addressing fatigue caused by prolonged screen use and decreased attention. The qualitative methodology included four focus groups with fifteen English Language Teaching students, whose transcriptions were analyzed using Atlas.ti. The results revealed mental and physical exhaustion, as well as reduced concentration due to continuous exposure and excessive academic activities. The conclusions emphasize the importance of regulating exposure time, promoting breaks, and encouraging digital disconnection, combining these strategies with flexible pedagogical approaches that balance the digital and the human dimensions to foster healthier learning experiences (c) 2026 Ochoa Guti & eacute;rrez, Guti & eacute;rrez Guti & eacute;rrez, & Carretero Hern & aacute;ndez. TI Development of Augmented Reality-Based Learning Modules to Improve
   Student Achievement and Motivation in Isometric Transformations
SO BULLETIN OF THE TECHNICAL COMMITTEE ON LEARNING TECHNOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE learning module; augmented reality; motivation; achievement
ID MATHEMATICS
AB This study investigates the effectiveness of an augmented reality (AR)-based learning module (ISOMAR) on student achievement and motivation in Isometric Transformations. Using a Design and Development Research (DDR) approach, the study involved 95 Form 2 students from Malaysia, who were randomly assigned to three groups: the ISOMAR group (AR-based module), the ISOMAX group (non-AR module), and a control group (conventional teaching method). Student achievement was assessed via pre-and post-tests, while motivation was measured using the Instructional Materials Motivation Survey (IMMS), which evaluates four constructs: attention, relevance, confidence, and satisfaction. ANCOVA, with pre-test scores as covariates, revealed a significant difference in achievement across groups, with the ISOMAR group outperforming both the ISOMAX and control groups. MANOVA results further indicated that students in the ISOMAR group reported significantly higher levels of attention, relevance, confidence, and satisfaction. These findings suggest that AR-based learning can effectively enhance both motivation and academic performance in Isometric Transformations.

TI Teaching practices in the humanities and social sciences at the
   elementary level in Quebec 25 years after the curriculum reform
SO EDUCACAO & FORMACAO
LA English
DT Article
DE teaching practices; humanities and social sciences; elementary
   education; didactics
AB Introduction. This article explores teaching practices in the humanities and social sciences at the elementary school level, 25 years after the curriculum and teacher education reform in Quebec. Methodology. The study draws on analysis of an online survey administered to 243 teachers to highlight the didactic dimensions of social studies teaching. Results and discussion. The results indicate that current practices prioritize the transmission of general knowledge in geography and history, as well as the development of attitudes and values to foster a sense of belonging in students. Although a research-based approach to history and geography teaching has been partly incorporated, the instructional tools employed remain primarily focused on general knowledge, with limited use of didactic tools such as mind maps and concept maps. This situation reveals a significant gap between available teaching resources and intended learning objectives, and highlights the need to revise practices in order to better align teaching with educational guidelines.

LA English
DT Article

AB Introduction. Linguistic Communication Competence is distinguished by its cross-curricular nature, which makes it essential for academic success in any subject area and for the holistic development of students, a fact supported by Spain's legal and regulatory framework for education. TI The impact of virtual reality on lexical recognition in English : a
   comparative study
SO EDUCACION XX1
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE virtual environments; vocabulary skills; English as a Foreign Language
   Learning; cognitive process; secondary education; comparative study
ID EDUCATION
AB Technology plays a fundamental role in foreign language teaching by providing didactic tools aimed at enhancing students' motivation and performance. Among these, virtual reality has emerged as a promising pedagogical resource, with an exponential increase in research on its impact since 2015. However, in order to accurately assess its effects on foreign language learning, it is essential to observe and analyze its integration and use in real educational contexts. This study examines the impact of 360 degrees immersive learning, using a virtual reality headset, on lexical recognition in English as a foreign language. To this end, a comparative experiment was conducted with three cohorts of 124 French participants between 2019 and 2021. The participants were equally assigned to two experimental conditions: an immersive learning experimental group and a non-immersive learning control group. The research protocol consisted of three phases: a pre-test to ensure the initial homogeneity of participants in terms of lexical level, a learning phase using one of the two VR modalities, and a post-test to assess participants' lexical recognition performance. The results revealed significant differences between the two learning modalities: in all three cohorts, participants in the experimental group consistently achieved significantly better results than those in the control group. These findings suggest that immersive environments, both in 3D and 360 degrees, can enhance foreign language learning by optimizing the cognitive processes involved in vocabulary acquisition and retention. These results may be attributed to a higher level of attention, motivation, and sense of presence experienced during the immersive learning process. Sensory interaction and the feeling of presence seem to promote active engagement and better consolidation of the learned vocabulary.

TI Transition and retention in tourism programs: impact of pedagogical
   innovation in a Mexican university
SO EDUCACION XX1
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE academic support; higher education; learning outcomes; student
   satisfaction; tourism higher education
AB Transition and retention in higher education pose significant challenges for Mexican educational institutions, particularly in professional programs such as the Tourism degree. This study analyzes the relationship between pedagogical innovation, student satisfaction, and academic performance, considering the mediating role of competency development and institutional support. A quantitative, cross-sectional, correlational design was applied to a sample of 222 students enrolled in the Tourism Educational Program at a public university in Mexico. A validated questionnaire was used, structured into four dimensions: competency development, university transition, pedagogical innovation, and support services. Data were analyzed through structural equation modeling. Pedagogical innovation and institutional support services emerged as significant predictors of student satisfaction (R-2 = 0.68). The model showed satisfactory fit indices (CFI = .93; RMSEA = .05) and confirmed an indirect influence on academic performance mediated by competency development (beta = .13, p < .01). A negative correlation was also identified between age and academic performance (r = -.24, p < .01). The findings highlight the importance of integrating pedagogical innovation with academic support strategies to enhance the university experience. Low scores in language programs and university transition processes reveal areas for improvement. A limitation of the study lies in its single-institution application, which restricts generalization. Future research should extend this analysis through multi-site and mixed-method approaches.

TI Private female agricultural education in Chile between 1950 and 1970:
   female models and international influences in rural education
SO HISTORIA Y MEMORIA DE LA EDUCACION
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Female agricultural education; Private education; Chile; History of
   rural education
AB The education of women who lived in rural areas and were involved in agricultural work is a topic that has been scarcely addressed by Chilean educational historiography. In this article, we propose to shed light on and analyze the female agricultural training initiative put forth by the Dolores Vald & eacute;s de Covarrubias Foundation, a private institution associated with the Catholic University. We will examine its founding principles and operational framework. Our proposal posits that the Foundation, along with its nearly ten womens' agricultural schools, filled a void in educational provision that the Ministry of Public Education had not addressed. Additionally, we argue that both the schools' functioning and the models it transmitted, rooted in religious principles, were influenced by Catholic Womens' Action and the rural education paradigms of Francos' Spain. These models were geared towards preparing women for their roles as wives, mothers, and managers of peasant households. This research draws primarily from documentation sourced from the Rural Life Foundations of the Historical Archive of the Catholic University, records from the Ministry of Public Education housed in the National Archive of the Administration of Chile, and international correspondence from the Womens' Section of FET and the JONS (Traditionalist Spanish Falange and the National Unionist Offensive Boards) from the General Archive of the Administration of Spain.

AB Fundamental education was a programme introduced by UNESCO between the mid-1940s and the late 1950s that aimed to provide populations in areas assumed as disadvantaged with the minimum tools needed to improve their living conditions through their own means. This approach stemmed from an amalgam of colonial, rural, and mass educational experiences, and involved several actors with different perspectives on education and its role in social change. TI Female Education in the Democratic six-year period. An approach to the
   discourses and practices of Republicanism (1868-1874)
SO HISTORIA Y MEMORIA DE LA EDUCACION
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE Republicanism; Female education; History of education; Spanish
   democratic Sexennium
AB The Spanish Democratic six-year period represented a certain educational revolution marked by new initiatives, both formal and non-formal, carried out by social groups that had not previously been the preferred focus of educational policy, such as republicanism, the labor movement or women themselves. The education of women prior to this period was characterized by being poor and domestic, directed towards their essential social functions: motherhood and marriage. However, the socio-political changes of the moment fostered transformations in the discourse around the education of the fair sex, from both the male and female sectors of the republican political culture. In the speeches of the Republican men, new educational experiences were advocated for their female companions whose ultimate goal was to maintain the ideas of progress, secularism or social justice in the family, regenerate the nation, promote access to professional space or expand their female educational level. On the other hand, republican women began to think about their situation of subordination and demand the necessary improvements in their education with the aim of achieving social regeneration and access to professions that would allow them to maintain greater levels of autonomy, without yet considering their emancipation. In short, these women maintained the republican ideology, redefining it based on their experience and creating new discourses that opened slight gaps in the current models of female identities, in their context.

TI ENGAGING WITH TRANSNATIONAL EDUCATIONAL IDEAS IN AN ERA OF INSULATION
   AND ISOLATION: IRISH EDUCATION POLICY FROM THE MID-1930s TO THE END OF
   THE 1950s
SO HISTORIA Y MEMORIA DE LA EDUCACION
LA English
DT Article
DE Ireland; Schooling; Curriculum; Physical education; Transnational
   knowledge circulation
ID BRITISH INFLUENCE
AB The period from the mid-1930s to the end of the 1950s has been characterised as one when Ireland was largely insulated and isolated on various fronts from the wider world. Much of the analysis in history of education research to date has focused on the efforts of the partners in the provision of education, namely, the Catholic Church and the State, to look inwards in search of models to inform their efforts to imbue future generations through schooling with a loyalty and deference to Catholic teachings, and to build nationhood and national identity. This article, which explores two key education policies in the period, is offered as an effort towards indicating how this deficit could be addressed by conducting wider studies along the same lines. Those who promoted one of the policies, that on physical education, drew upon transnational influences to indicate what they perceived as developments that needed to be undertaken to advance the subject in schools. Those who promoted the other policy, that on restricting the teaching of sex education in schools, justified the position they adopted by regularly referencing a different set of transnational influences.

Beyond the analyzed texts, it is relevant to highlight the dialogue between tradition and modernity.

TI Internationalising the production of school textbooks. Dialogues and
   Tensions in the Chilean Typographic Space (1860-1884)
SO HISTORIA Y MEMORIA DE LA EDUCACION
LA Spanish
DT Article
DE School textbooks; Typographic industry; Chile; 19th century
AB This article analyses the function of the Chilean typographic space and the market for school textbooks between 1860 and 1884. It examines the content of the educational reforms imposed during the 1860s regarding the production and distribution of printed material for education and their impact on the national printing market. Thus, it is proposed that the businessmen in the field encouraged the modernisation and specialisation of the industry, as they saw in these printed materials an effective means for the survival of their workshops, since they guaranteed a constant source of income. However, infrastructural limitations did not allow the growing demand for books to be met locally, which led to the internationalisation of the textbook production process. The signing of contracts with European and American publishers and printers ensured a cheaper and more expeditious supply, which affected national imprints that were unable to compete in the didactic bibliography market. This phenomenon generated tensions within the local industry, as entrepreneurs and workers saw the sustainability of the national workshops threatened. The study examines, from a perspective that focuses on the material dimension of the book, contracts between printers and the state, legal disputes, educational legislation and the workers' press in order to understand the functioning of the textbook market, the actors involved in it at various levels (local, regional, international) and their ways of relating to each other.

TI AI-Generated Microlearning for Plastic Surgery Residency: Single-Arm
   Pre-Post Feasibility Study
SO JMIR MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE artificial intelligence; graduate medical education; plastic surgery;
   microlearning; large language models; feasibility studies;
   multiple-choice questions
ID MEDICAL-EDUCATION; RESTRICTIONS
AB Background: Surgical residency training faces mounting pressure from expanding subspecialty knowledge requirements alongside compressed learning opportunities. Microlearning, defined as brief, focused educational episodes, offers a pedagogically sound approach suited to fragmented clinical schedules, while large language models present capabilities for scalable content generation. However, the feasibility, quality, and educational value of large language model-generated microlearning in surgical training remain unexplored. Objective: This study aimed to assess the feasibility and acceptability of artificial intelligence (AI)-generated microlearning modules among plastic surgery residents, evaluate content quality through systematic faculty evaluation, and generate preliminary effect size estimates for self-perceived knowledge and confidence changes. Methods: A single-arm pilot feasibility study with a pre-post design was conducted at an academic plastic surgery residency program (N=11 residents) over 12 weeks. Six modules covering core subspecialties were developed using Google Gemini 2.5 Pro. From 60 AI-generated multiple-choice questions, 42 were selected following independent evaluation by 2 board-certified plastic surgeons using a 5-dimension rubric (accuracy, relevance, clarity, pedagogical value, and safety). Modules were released biweekly via Google Forms. Outcomes included retention, acceptability (7-point Likert scales), faculty evaluation ratings, item-level psychometrics, and pre-post changes in self-perceived knowledge and confidence. Composite scores were calculated as the mean change across all 6 subspecialty topics. Wilcoxon signed-rank tests served as the primary analysis for matched pairs Results: All 11 residents completed postassessments. Acceptability was high across all 6 subitems (all medians >= 5 out of 7). Faculty evaluation confirmed high content quality (mean quality index 4.68/5); interrater reliability was poor (intraclass correlation coefficient (3,1)=0.231). Among 9 matched pairs, composite confidence improved significantly (median change 0.33; d=0.65; P=.047), while composite knowledge showed a medium effect (d=0.71; P=.09). Topic-specific gains were largest where baseline was lowest: hand surgery knowledge (d=1.48; P=.02) and confidence (d=1.41; P=.02). Resource use and sense-of-community measures remained stable. Conclusions: AI-generated microlearning modules are feasible and acceptable for plastic surgery residency education. Faculty-evaluated content achieved high quality ratings (mean 4.68/5), and residents showed strong engagement with preliminary improvements in self-perceived confidence. The intervention was integrated into existing learning ecosystems without disrupting traditional resources or peer dynamics. These findings provide effect size estimates to support the design of adequately powered randomized trials.

TI e-Learning, Distance Education, and Virtual and Augmented Reality in
   Orthopedic Training: European Cross-Sectional Survey of Trainee
   Acceptance Guided by the Technology Acceptance Model and Unified Theory
   of Acceptance and Use of Technology
SO JMIR MEDICAL EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE augmented reality; digital learning; distance education; e-learning;
   medical education; orthopedic training; virtual reality
ID HEALTH-PROFESSIONS; SIMULATOR; ATTITUDE; SURGERY
AB Background: Digital technologies increasingly shape postgraduate medical education, yet orthopedic and trauma training face unique challenges because of the tactile, procedurally focused skills involved. Digital tools partially address these needs, but gaps remain, particularly across diverse European contexts. Objective: Our primary aim was to quantitatively assess predictors of digital learning technology acceptance (e-learning, distance education, and virtual reality [VR] and augmented reality [AR]) among European orthopedic and trauma trainees, drawing on the technology acceptance model (TAM) and the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT) as conceptual guides. Specifically, weexamined how perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use (TAM), alongside performanceexpectancy, effortexpectancy, social influence, and facilitatingconditions (UTAUT), related totrainees' acceptance of digital technologies. These constructs guided variable selection and grouping, attitudinal scale design, and interpretation of how individual and contextual factors shape acceptance of digital learning tools in orthopedic training. Secondary aims were to describe adoption and attitude patterns, identify attitudinal trainee profiles, and examine contextual associations (eg, workplace type and national gross domestic product [GDP]). Methods: We distributed a multinational survey via European trainee federations and used validated scales to assess digital competence and attitudes and gathered demographic data (n=217 across 29 European countries). We administered the questionnaire in English; however, respondents who self-reported English proficiency below the intermediate level were excluded from the analyses to minimize potential comprehension-related bias. The survey assessed digital experience, self-reported digital competence, and attitudes toward e-learning, distance education, and VR/AR, and collected detailed demographic and workplace data. Expert review, cognitive pretesting, and pilot testing ensured validity and clarity. Analytical methods included Wilcoxon tests, ANOVA, clustering, multinomial logistic regression, and factor analysis to ensure the reliability and validity of attitudinal measures. Results: e-Learning technologies were the most widely adopted, whereasVR/AR tools were less frequently used despite high average attitude ratings (mean 4.07, SD 0.88). Cluster analysis identified 3 distinctive groups-enthusiastic, supportive, and hesitant-that differed significantly in digital competence and acceptance profiles. Digital competence and national GDP emerged as significant predictors of group membership, consistent with TAM/UTAUT expectations that perceived capability and contextual facilitating conditions shape acceptance. Variation in attitudes was further associated with workplace type and regional resource disparities, underscoring the influence of contextual factors on technology adoption. Conclusions: European orthopedic trainees show broad support for digital innovations, preferring VR/AR despite low use. Preliminary evidence supports digital competence as a key mediator of acceptance, with GDP and workplace disparities predicting profiles (hesitant vs enthusiastic). Competence-first strategies and targeted resource equity (eg, low-GDP subsidies), together with policy adjustments, may address regional disparities. Future longitudinal and multimethod studies are needed to test causal pathways implied by TAM and UTAUT and to evaluate the generalizability of these findings across specialties and educational contexts.

TI Chiropractic students' perceived preparedness in diagnosing and managing
   headache disorders at a selected university
SO JOURNAL OF CHIROPRACTIC EDUCATION
LA English
DT Article
DE Headache; Confidence; Education; Self-Perceived Preparedness
ID MANAGEMENT
AB Objective: To explore and describe master's chiropractic students' self-perceived preparedness in diagnosing and managing head-ache disorders. Methods: A qualitative, exploratory, descriptive design was used. Thirteen master's chiropractic students participated in semi-structured interviews guided by an interview protocol. Interviews were thematically analyzed using Tesch's 8-step approach. Results: Participants reported and expressed limited preparedness and low initial confidence in diagnosing and managing head-ache disorders. Conclusion: The exploration of students' self-perceived preparedness in diagnosing and managing headache disorders identified multiple contributing factors. Educational and environmental challenges were associated with feelings of limited preparedness. However, increased clinical exposure enhanced both confidence and perceived competence.

TI AI-generated versus teacher feedback: A comparative study on EFL
   learners' public speaking anxiety and oral presentation performance
SO LANGUAGE LEARNING & TECHNOLOGY
LA English
DT Article
DE public speaking anxiety; AI feedback; teacher feedback; oral
   presentation performance; EFL learners
ID ARTIFICIAL-INTELLIGENCE; ENGLISH PRONUNCIATION
AB This comparative study investigates the impact of artificial intelligence (AI)-generated feedback versus teacher-provided feedback on public speaking anxiety (PSA) and oral presentation performance among Turkish EFL learners. Adopting a quasi-experimental pre-test-post-test control group research design, thirty university students took part in the study. They were assigned to either an experimental group receiving AI feedback or a control group receiving teacher feedback. Over five weeks, participants delivered presentations and received feedback based on their group assignment. Quantitative data were collected through the Public Speaking Anxiety Scale (PSAS) to measure anxiety levels and a standardized rubric to evaluate oral presentation performance. The findings showed that both feedback types significantly decreased students' public speaking anxiety and improved their presentation skills. Specifically, AI-generated feedback resulted in a notably greater reduction in PSA, whereas both groups achieved similar improvements in oral performance. Qualitative data from interviews with AI group participants supported the quantitative findings, underlining increased self-awareness, practical guidance, and enhanced confidence. The study concludes that while both feedback sources are effective for skill development, AI-generated feedback holds a distinct advantage in decreasing public speaking anxiety. This underlines the value of AI as a complementary tool in EFL speaking instruction, supporting a hybrid pedagogical model that harnesses the strengths of both automated and human feedback.

TI AN EXPERIMENT SIMULATING CORPORATE TRAINING USING BUSINESS PROCESS
   MODELS
SO MATHEMATICS AND INFORMATICS
LA English
DT Article
DE business processes; BPMN; corporate training; corporate hierarchy;
   employee training simulation
ID CONTEXT
AB The article examines the application of business processes in the design and implementation of corporate strategy for employee's professional development. A training approach using processes in an organization is presented, which allows for the definition and unambiguous formalization of a learning goal and the learning path for its achievement. A model of a corporate hierarchy is used, represented by a tree structure of roles, implemented in cloud space. Each role is attached to the business processes in which it participates.
